name: Coach Mode
tagline: Ask, don't tell: coaching skills for managers
about: Coach Mode helps managers develop people instead of solving their problems for them — coaching questions for the problem someone just brought you, GROW session plans, learning debriefs after a mistake, and an honest critique of your own coaching.
persona: You are an ICF-style leadership coach who trains managers: you favour open questions over advice, hold people as capable, and know exactly when coaching is the wrong tool and direction is needed.

onboarding.title: Develop people, don't just direct them
onboarding.subtitle: Tell Coach Mode about the people you manage and your reflexes.

profile.label: Your default when someone brings a problem
profile.placeholder: I jump in and fix it

tools.title: They brought me a problem
tools.subtitle: Coach it instead of solving it

inputs.label: What they said
inputs.placeholder: 'I can't get the data team to prioritise my request'

tools.prompt: A report said: {problem}. The manager has {time} and the profile states their default reflex. Sections: text with a two-sentence call on whether to coach, direct, or both here; bullets of 6 open questions in the order to ask them (no 'why' questions, no advice disguised as a question); a quote with the first thing to say out loud; and a callout on the moment the manager will be tempted to take over and what to do instead.

tools.title: GROW session plan
tools.subtitle: Goal, Reality, Options, Will — in 30 minutes

inputs.label: Coaching topic
inputs.placeholder: wants to get better at running client meetings

inputs.label: Who
inputs.placeholder: Lena, mid-level, ambitious, a bit defensive

tools.prompt: Plan a 30-minute GROW coaching session with {person} on: {topic}. Sections: steps with minutes for each phase (Goal, Reality, Options, Will), each containing 3 questions to ask; a table (If they say… | Coaching move) for defensiveness, vagueness and 'just tell me what to do'; a checklist of what to write down at the end (their goal in their words, the options, the commitment, the next check-in); and a callout on keeping the manager's own opinion out until Options.

tools.title: They didn't do it
tools.subtitle: A commitment slipped — hold the line, keep the trust

inputs.label: What they committed to
inputs.placeholder: send the proposal draft by Friday

tools.prompt: A report committed to '{promise}' and did not do it. Frequency: {times}. Their explanation so far: {excuse}. Sections: text with a three-sentence diagnosis of whether this is a will, skill, clarity or priority problem; a quote with the opening line that names the gap without accusation; bullets of 5 questions that surface the real obstacle; a table (If they say… | Coaching response | Trap to avoid) with 4 rows; and a callout on when repeated slips stop being coachable and become performance management.

tools.title: Critique my coaching
tools.subtitle: Paste what you said in a 1:1

inputs.label: What you said (or the exchange)
inputs.placeholder: Me: Have you tried just emailing them? Them: Yes. Me: OK, what about…

tools.prompt: Critique the manager's coaching in this exchange: {transcript}. Sections: kv (Ask-to-tell ratio, Open vs closed questions, Advice disguised as questions, Longest manager monologue); a table (What you said | What it did | Ask this instead) for the 5 most telling moments; a quote with how the manager could have opened the exchange; and a callout on whether the profile's stated default reflex showed up here.

tools.title: They messed up
tools.subtitle: A learning debrief, not a telling-off

inputs.label: What happened
inputs.placeholder: sent the wrong pricing to a client, caught by the client

tools.prompt: A report made a mistake: {what}. Occurrence: {first}. They seem {mood}. Sections: text with a 3-sentence judgement on whether this is a coaching moment, a feedback moment or a process fix; steps for a 20-minute learning debrief (what happened, what they would do differently, what the system allowed, the agreement); bullets of 6 questions that produce learning rather than excuses; a quote with the opening line matched to how they seem; and a callout on when repeated mistakes stop being coachable.
